verses.text: Once we were safely ashore, we found out the island’s name: Malta.
The islanders showed us serious kindness. They lit a fire and welcomed the whole crew, because rain was coming down and it was cold.
Paul gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire. The heat drove out a viper, and it clamped onto his hand.
When the islanders saw the snake hanging there, they said to each other, “This guy must be a murderer. He got away from the sea, but Justice still won’t let him live.”
But Paul shook the snake off into the fire and wasn’t hurt at all.
They expected him to swell up or drop dead any second. They waited a long time, saw nothing happen, and switched up: now they were saying he was a god.
Nearby were lands belonging to Publius, the island’s chief official. He welcomed us and hosted us generously for three days.
Publius’s father was sick in bed with fever and dysentery. Paul went in, prayed, laid his hands on him, and healed him.
After that, everybody else on the island who was sick came through and got healed too.
They showed us a lot of respect. When we were ready to sail, they loaded the ship with what we needed.
Three months later, we sailed on an Alexandrian ship that had spent winter on the island. Its figurehead was the Twin Brothers.
We docked at Syracuse and stayed three days.
Then we sailed around to Rhegium. A day later a south wind came up, and the next day we reached Puteoli,
where we found believers who invited us to stay with them for a week. After that, we headed to Rome.
The believers in Rome heard we were coming and came out to meet us at the Market of Appius and the Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and felt encouraged.
When we got into Rome, the centurion handed the prisoners over to the captain of the guard. Paul got permission to stay by himself, with a soldier keeping watch.

Three days later, Paul called in the Jewish leaders. When they arrived, he said, “Brothers, I haven’t done anything against our people or our ancestors’ customs. Still, I was arrested in Jerusalem and handed over to the Romans,
“who questioned me and wanted to set me free, because they found nothing I’d done that deserved death.
“But the Jewish leaders pushed back, so I had to appeal to Caesar. I’m not accusing my own people of anything.
“That’s why I asked to see you and talk this through. I’m wearing this chain because of Israel’s hope.”
They said, “We haven’t received letters about you from Judea, and none of our people have come here with a bad report.
“But we do want to hear what you think. We know people everywhere talk against this movement.”
They picked a day, and a crowd came to Paul’s place. From morning till night he laid it out for them, testifying about God’s Kingdom and making the case for Jesus from Moses’ Law and the Prophets.
Some were convinced; others weren’t buying it.
They couldn’t agree, so they started heading out after Paul said one last thing: “The Holy Spirit got it right when he spoke to our ancestors through Isaiah the prophet:
“‘Go tell this people: You’ll hear and hear but never understand; you’ll look and look but never see.
“‘Their hearts have gone hard. Their ears barely hear, and they’ve shut their eyes. Otherwise, they could see, hear, understand in their hearts, turn back, and I would heal them.’”
“So know this: God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen.”
After he said that, the Jewish visitors left, arguing among themselves.
Paul stayed two full years in his rented home and welcomed everybody who came to see him.
He kept preaching God’s Kingdom and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ—with full boldness, and nobody shut him down. 🙌
